strategies.title: Deterministic annealed max-ratio search
strategies.plan: Replace the random Gaussian cloud with a deterministic best-so-far direct search initialized from the 16-point triangular-lattice hexagon obtained by deleting alternating corners from the 19-point radius-two hexagonal cluster.  Evaluate the actual squared objective, `min(pairwise_squared_distances) / max(pairwise_squared_distances)`, after each proposal rather than optimizing a surrogate.  Use a fixed-seed annealing phase that proposes both single-point displacements and occasional coordinated all-point perturbations, accepts improving proposals unconditionally, permits controlled temporary losses early, and retains the best state ever seen.  Follow that with deterministic decreasing-step coordinate/pattern refinement that accepts only strict objective improvements.  Preserve validity by always returning the retained 16-by-2 best array; translation and scale are immaterial, and the fallback lattice has no coincident points.  The checkable fallback has raw `min_max_ratio = 1/13`, hence combined score `(1/13)/(1/12.889266112)=12.889266112/13=0.9914820086>0.0197911238456`, while the direct best-so-far search is predicted to cross the supplied target and give predicted `combined_score > 1 > 0.0197911238456`.

strategies.title: Alternating-corner hexagonal cluster
strategies.plan: Use the unit triangular lattice with basis vectors `(1,0)` and `(1/2,sqrt(3)/2)`, taking all axial lattice coordinates `(q,r)` satisfying `max(abs(q), abs(r), abs(q+r)) <= 2`.  This gives the familiar 19-point hexagonal cluster with nearest-neighbor distance exactly one.  Delete the three alternating outer corners `(2,0)`, `(0,-2)`, and `(-2,2)`, leaving exactly 16 points.  Every retained pair is a distinct triangular-lattice pair, so the minimum distance is one, while direct enumeration of the retained axial differences gives maximum squared Euclidean distance 13.  This is a mesoscopic replacement of the unstructured random cloud by a compact near-isotropic packing and needs no iterative solver.  The exact raw objective is `1/13`, so the predicted `combined_score=(1/13)/(1/12.889266112)=0.9914820086>0.0197911238456`.

strategies.title: Contact-graph local polishing
strategies.plan: Start from the alternating-corner hexagonal cluster and retain its current best point set as an always-valid fallback.  At each deterministic sweep, identify all pairs attaining the current minimum distance and all pairs within a small tolerance of the current diameter.  Move one point at a time along the normalized sum of repulsive unit vectors from minimum-distance contacts plus attractive unit vectors toward the centroid of its diameter partners, then accept the move only if the actual squared min/max ratio strictly increases.  Use a fixed sequence of decreasing step sizes, and perform the same accepted-move test after every update, so no accepted operation can degrade the measured score.  The output remains exactly 16 finite 2D coordinates throughout, and rejection preserves the previous valid state.  The valid no-improvement fallback has raw `min_max_ratio=1/13`, hence predicted fallback `combined_score=12.889266112/13=0.9914820086>0.0197911238456`.

strategies.title: Active-contact force polishing
strategies.plan: Keep the incumbent triangular-cluster annealing construction, but replace the final coarse eight-direction-only polish with an active-contact refinement that explicitly uses the pairs attaining, or nearly attaining, the current minimum and maximum squared distances. For each point, form a deterministic force that pushes active minimum-distance neighbors apart and pulls active diameter-pair endpoints together; test both signs and a fixed geometric sequence of step lengths, retaining only strict objective gains. Follow each accepted collective move with per-point searches over 24 evenly spaced angular directions, including steps below the incumbent’s final 0.0014 scale, so diagonal and non-axis-aligned contact motions are available. Preserve the best annealed point array as an unconditional fallback, and accept a candidate only when the exact same `min(v)/max(v)` calculation is strictly larger, so point count, dimension, and all pairwise factors used by scoring remain unchanged. The expected-gain check is that the implementation evaluates the exact incumbent plus strict active-contact candidates and returns the best valid array; the forecast raw objective is 0.07763, which converts as `0.07763 / (1/12.889266112) = 1.00059`, strictly above the current 0.993968 combined score.

strategies.title: Boundary-block replacement beam
strategies.plan: Use the annealed incumbent as a fixed 12-point core, identify the four points with the largest incidence among near-diameter pairs and near-minimum pairs, and replace that four-point boundary subsystem jointly rather than moving one point at a time. Generate each replacement point from a deterministic polar stencil around the core centroid: 24 angles, radii equal to the current radial distance times `0.92, 0.96, 1.00, 1.04, 1.08`, plus the original four locations. Build the four-point subsystem greedily with a beam of the best 32 partial replacements under the exact global ratio, requiring distinct stencil locations, then run a short local angular polish on the surviving full arrays. Repeat for the three deterministic choices of four boundary points induced by sorting contact incidence, always retaining the original array if no replacement improves it. This is a mesoscopic move because it can change the outer contact graph and the diameter endpoints together while the interior packing scaffold remains stable. The expected-gain check is that every beam survivor and polish move is scored by the exact incumbent objective with strict acceptance and an incumbent fallback; the forecast raw objective is 0.07766, giving `0.07766 / (1/12.889266112) = 1.00098`, strictly above the current 0.993968 combined score.

strategies.title: Three-orbit shell exploration
strategies.plan: Add a structurally independent family based on a 16-point dihedral shell decomposition: one center point, a 3-point equilateral orbit, and two 6-point regular or phase-shifted hexagonal orbits. Parameterize it explicitly by the three radii and the two orbit phases: center `(0,0)`, triangle points `r1*(cos(phi1+2*pi*k/3), sin(phi1+2*pi*k/3))`, and two hexagons `rj*(cos(phij+2*pi*k/6), sin(phij+2*pi*k/6))`; normalize the outer radius to one. Search the five parameters on deterministic nested grids, first with radius increments 0.02 and phase increments `pi/60`, then halve both increments twice around the best cell, and finally release symmetry with the same active-contact local polish used on the selected shell. Compare this shell family, the triangular-lattice incumbent, and the refined shell using the same exact ratio, so no assumption that symmetry is beneficial can degrade the output. The construction is always a finite `(16,2)` NumPy array with unique angular samples and has an incumbent fallback, hence it preserves all hard constraints. The expected-gain check is that the shell candidate is retained only after an exact strict ratio comparison against the incumbent and otherwise the incumbent is returned; the forecast raw objective is 0.07770, giving `0.07770 / (1/12.889266112) = 1.00149`, strictly above the current 0.993968 combined score.
